summary: The Arabic adjective comes AFTER its noun and copies four things from it: gender, number, case and definiteness — بَيْتٌ كَبِيرٌ (a big house), الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ (the big house), غُرْفَةٌ صَغِيرَةٌ (a small room), فِي الْبَيْتِ الْكَبِيرِ (in the big house), أُرِيدُ كِتَابًا جَدِيدًا (I want a new book). The feminine adds ـَة; the dual ends in -āni / -ayni (سَيَّارَتَانِ جَدِيدَتَانِ). The article decides between a phrase and a sentence: with al- on both words it is “the big house”; with al- only on the noun it is the verbless sentence “the house is big”, الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ (lesson 1). A noun with an owner ending is definite, so its adjective takes al-: بَيْتِي الْكَبِيرُ (my big house). Plurals of things take the feminine singular (الْبُيُوتُ كَبِيرَةٌ, الْكُتُبُ الْجَدِيدَةُ); plurals of people take a plural adjective, often a broken one (أَطْفَالٌ صِغَارٌ, طُلَّابٌ جُدُدٌ) or the sound -ūna (مُتْعَبُونَ). After لَيْسَ and كَانَ the predicate adjective is accusative: الْبَيْتُ لَيْسَ كَبِيرًا. A few adjectives have shapes of their own: عَطْشَانُ / عَطْشَى (no tanwīn), the defective غَالٍ / غَالِيًا / الْغَالِي, and the colours of lesson 17.

blocks.title: Things in the plural are “she” — also for adjectives.
blocks.text: الْبُيُوتُ كَبِيرَةٌ (the houses are big), السَّيَّارَاتُ الْجَدِيدَةُ (the new cars), الْكُتُبُ الْقَدِيمَةُ (the old books). Plural adjectives are for people only: الْأَطْفَالُ صِغَارٌ, نَحْنُ سُعَدَاءُ.

blocks.title: The article: on both words, or the sentence changes.
blocks.text: الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ = the big house; الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ = the house is big. Never *بَيْتٌ الْكَبِيرُ or *الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرُ.

blocks.title: After لَيْسَ and كَانَ: accusative.
blocks.text: الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ → الْبَيْتُ لَيْسَ كَبِيرًا (is not big) — كَانَ الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرًا (was big). The same with feelings: لَسْتُ مُتْعَبًا (I’m not tired).

blocks.title: Two adjectives.
blocks.text: They follow one another, each agreeing: بَيْتٌ كَبِيرٌ جَمِيلٌ (a big, beautiful house), or with وَ: الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ وَجَمِيلٌ.

items: one, two, several — people or things?
blocks.caption: Choosing the form of an adjective.

blocks.text: Feelings are adjectives too, and they agree with the speaker: a man says أَنَا جَائِعٌ / مُتْعَبٌ / سَعِيدٌ, a woman أَنَا جَائِعَةٌ / مُتْعَبَةٌ / سَعِيدَةٌ. Two exceptions to remember: “I’m cold” is أَشْعُرُ بِالْبَرْدِ (not أَنَا بَارِدٌ), and “I’m fine” is أَنَا بِخَيْرٍ (not أَنَا جَيِّدٌ).

askYourself: Does it describe the noun (a big house) or say something about it (the house is big)?
Is the noun definite — al-, an owner ending, a name? → the adjective takes al- too (for a description).
Masculine or feminine? → feminine: ـَة (or a special shape: عَطْشَى).
People or things? Things in the plural → feminine singular.
People in the plural → which plural does this adjective have (كِبَار, جُدُد … or -ūna)?
Which case is the noun in — subject, object, after a preposition? The adjective copies it.
Is it the predicate after لَيْسَ or كَانَ? → accusative (كَبِيرًا).

traps: “The house is big” is الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ, not *الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ (that is “the big house”).
Things in the plural: الْكُتُبُ جَدِيدَةٌ, not *الْكُتُبُ جُدُدٌ.
After a preposition the adjective is genitive too: فِي الْبَيْتِ الْكَبِيرِ, not *الْكَبِيرُ.
“My big house” is بَيْتِي الْكَبِيرُ; بَيْتِي كَبِيرٌ means “my house is big”.
A woman is عَطْشَى (or عَطْشَانَة), not *عَطْشَانُ; the masculine has no tanwīn: عَطْشَانُ.
Old people are مُسِنّ / كَبِيرٌ فِي السِّنِّ — قَدِيم is for things.
The predicate after لَيْسَ is accusative: الْبَيْتُ لَيْسَ كَبِيرًا.

quiz.why: A description takes al- like its noun; الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ is the sentence “the house is big”.
Things in the plural take the feminine singular.
After the noun, feminine like غُرْفَة.
People in the plural take a plural adjective — here the broken plural جِيَاع.
The adjective copies the genitive and the article.
Indefinite nominative of the defective adjective: غَالٍ; الْهَاتِفُ الْغَالِي is “the expensive phone”.
The feminine of عَطْشَان is عَطْشَى (in speech عَطْشَانَة).
For people: مُسِنّ (or كَبِيرٌ فِي السِّنِّ); قَدِيم is for things.

seeAlso.note: Hebrew is the closest: the adjective follows the noun and repeats the article (הַבַּיִת הַגָּדוֹל, the big house; הַבַּיִת גָּדוֹל, the house is big), with four forms (גָּדוֹל, גְּדוֹלָה, גְּדוֹלִים, גְּדוֹלוֹת) — but no cases, no dual, and things in the plural stay plural (בָּתִּים גְּדוֹלִים).

German puts the adjective BEFORE the noun with strong / weak / mixed endings (ein großes Haus, das große Haus); a predicate never changes (das Haus ist groß) — in Arabic the predicate agrees too (الْغُرْفَةُ كَبِيرَةٌ).
Chinese adjectives are stative verbs: 房子很大 (the house is big — with 很), 大房子 or 很大的房子 before the noun with 的; no agreement at all.
The agreement rule of lesson 4 — things in the plural are feminine singular — now applies to adjectives.
الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ is a verbless sentence; كَانَ and لَيْسَ make the adjective accusative.
